• Built by the late and famous Gene Winfield
• Designed by the film's art department and hand-built by Gene Winfield, legendary Hollywood car customizer
• Based on a 1977 Oldsmobile Cutlass Supreme chassis, extensively re-bodied in fiberglass.
• Features exaggerated styling: triple rear exhausts, squared wheel arches, and futuristic fascia created to parody 1980s automotive excess
• Purchased directly from Gene Winfield by Movie Cars Central

Created by master customizer Gene Winfield for Paul Verhoeven's RoboCop (1987), the SUX 6000 was designed as a satirical symbol of Detroit's consumer culture in the film's dystopian future. Based on a 1977 Oldsmobile Cutlass Supreme chassis, the car was re-imagined in fiberglass with enlarged body panels, widened track, and triple-barrel rear exhausts to give it an overblown, "hyper-luxury" appearance. Several units were built for production, and this example - chassis no. 3M29R7R152619 - is a verified screen-used vehicle, directly acquired from Winfield himself. Long celebrated as one of the few surviving original RoboCop cars, it represents the intersection of Hollywood design satire and classic American craftsmanship.
Previously exhibited at the Petersen Automotive Museum, this SUX 6000 is now offered on a bill of sale, accompanied by a Certificate of Authenticity signed by Gene Winfield. The vehicle will require recommissioning prior to use.

Built by Dennis McCarthy and his Vehicle Effects team for Fast & Furious 4 (2009), this Buick GNX is one of the most complex stunt vehicles ever engineered for the series. Used extensively in the film's opening highway heist scene, where Dominic Toretto (Vin Diesel) chases and drives in reverse toward a moving tanker truck, the car was purpose-built for that sequence. The vehicle's configuration is completely inverted: the engine is mounted in the trunk, while steering, pedals, and driver controls are concealed in the rear seat area, allowing the stunt driver to perform high-speed reverse manoeuvres safely and convincingly. Retaining its production modifications and original construction details, after being part of the Volo Auto Museum, the GNX was later acquired from a private collector in Europe and remains a remarkable piece of Fast & Furious stunt engineering.
Sold on a bill of sale and accompanied by a certificate from the Volo Auto Museum, this car is a genuine prop item and is not intended for road use.

Alongside the legendary Supra, Skyline, Evo, Charger, and all of Paul Walker's and Vin Diesel's cars, some supporting vehicles have also achieved cult status. Jesse's Jetta from the original movie is one such example, appearing prominently on-screen and later attracting media attention when the original car was acquired by Frankie Muniz of Malcolm in the Middle.
This 1993 Volkswagen Vento VR6—already a rare model—has been meticulously modified by a fan to create the closest possible replica of Jesse's Jetta. The car features a full body kit matching that of the movie car, a new white paint finish, and a complete sticker livery faithfully reproducing the original. It rides on correct König wheels, covering genuine brake calipers, and the suspension has been lowered for an authentic stance.
Inside, the interior has been upgraded with an aftermarket steering wheel, bucket seats, and a hi-fi system. Beneath the bonnet, performance enhancements include a Carbon Dynamics air intake, among other modifications. Acquired from its Spanish owner by Movie Cars Central, this vehicle is a well-known and much-admired member of the Museum collection.
Built with remarkable attention to detail, this Vento (Jetta) VR6 is offered with its Spanish title, making it a must-have for film enthusiasts and collectors alike. This car will require servicing prior to be driven.

Purchased around 2017 by Razorfly Studios—a renowned workshop celebrated in the United States for producing some of the finest movie-car replicas—this 1977 Chevrolet Camaro was selected as the basis for an accurate "Bumblebee" recreation. Starting with a restored example, the most challenging aspect was to reproduce the worn, aged appearance seen when Sam Witwicky first encounters Bumblebee in the 2007 Transformers film. Through skilful use of paint, the team created a remarkably convincing patina, capturing the character and charm of the on-screen car.
Matching the interior of the hero car was equally important. Bespoke vinyl materials were used, while memorable details—such as the mirrored facet-ball hanging from the rear-view mirror and the Autobots emblem on the steering wheel—were painstakingly reproduced to complete the transformation.
Sold with its US title and accompanied by its 846A customs document, this Camaro offers a rare opportunity to acquire one of the finest 'Bumblebee' replicas in Europe. Following mechanical recommissioning, it would make a wonderfully entertaining and highly characterful cruiser.

When the production of Drive (2011) began, Ryan Gosling was invited to choose a vehicle that would embody the quiet menace and mechanical precision of his character, known simply as "The Driver." The 1973 Chevrolet Chevelle Malibu became that car—a modest, slightly worn American muscle car that reflected the character's restraint and anonymity. Gosling is said to have personally helped prepare one of the film cars to better understand his role as a stunt driver and mechanic.
Three Chevelles were built for the production: one destroyed during stunt work, one retained by Gosling himself, and this example—used for hero driving and interior sequences. It appears in numerous scenes filmed around Los Angeles, including the film's haunting night drives and tense getaway moments. The car's interior remains unmistakable, with dashboard cracks that can be clearly matched to close-up shots of Gosling and Carey Mulligan on screen.
Retaining its production modifications, weathered primer-grey paint, and interior patina, this Chevelle remains exactly as it appeared on film—a tangible and evocative symbol of Nicolas Winding Refn's acclaimed neo-noir masterpiece.
Purchased by Movie Cars Central in January 2020 from a private collector in the United Kingdom, the car is accompanied by its Certificate of Authenticity signed by William "Billy" Powell, its previous UK V5 title, expired US title, and several related props from the film.
While complete, the car would require mechanical recommissioning prior to road use.

• Retains numerous production-specific features from filming, including stunt safety equipment, camera-rig mounting points, and screen-applied livery

When pre-production began on 2 Fast 2 Furious, the studio initially approached Nissan regarding product placement, before briefly considering the Opel Speedster. Neither option proved suitable for Brian O'Conner's character, and Mitsubishi ultimately entered into partnership with the production—supplying Eclipse Spyders and four Evolution VIIs.
The Evolutions presented a unique challenge. The Evo VII was not sold in the United States and was nearing the end of its model cycle; the Evo VIII, by contrast, would launch in the US shortly after the film's release. Mitsubishi therefore imposed a key requirement: the Evo VII used in the film had to resemble the forthcoming Evo VIII.
Eddie Paul Industries received four left-hand-drive Evo VIIs, originally finished in blue and diverted from an Austrian rally-team order. Converting them into "Evo VIII lookalikes" proved complex—particularly the rear lights. Mitsubishi could not provide pre-production Evo VIII components, so aftermarket clear-lens Lancer lights were sourced. These were not designed for the Evo's wide rear quarters, requiring the full reconstruction of the rear valance and explaining the noticeable spacing around the lights visible on screen.
Once the cars achieved the correct visual identity, the team selected a colour that would offer strong cinematic presence: Kosmic Kolor Candy Lime Gold. The shade was spectacular under lights, though difficult to repair quickly between takes—a challenge familiar to anyone who has worked with candy finishes.
All four Evolutions survived production and were later used for promotional events before passing into private hands.
This specific Evolution VII, chassis JMYSNCT9A1U000797, has been confirmed by Craig Lieberman as Stunt Car No. 1. It appears in multiple sequences throughout the film and is the only example upgraded mechanically, receiving enhanced turbocharging and suspension tuning for a verified output of 330 hp—making it the most performance-focused of the four cars. Each of the four Evolutions was built differently depending on its intended role: two featured neon lighting, one carried the Panasonic DVD player, and this car was the designated high-performance stunt unit.
The Evo VII is also among the most prominently featured vehicles in the entire Fast & Furious franchise, appearing on screen for nearly fifteen minutes. As one of Paul Walker's hero cars—and one which remained intact within the narrative—it is among the most desirable of the surviving franchise vehicles.
After filming, chassis 000797 is believed to have been used for promotional duties, during which it received Evo VIII seats and a later-style front bumper. Exported from the United States to Norway in 2007, the car appeared at numerous events before being acquired by Movie Cars Central in 2019. The original movie-used bumper was later rediscovered in a small Los Angeles workshop and has since been refitted, returning the car to its correct on-screen configuration.
Still displaying numerous production details from 2 Fast 2 Furious—including traces of its original blue paint visible in the boot and engine bay, as well as "FF3" stickers applied in several areas (suggesting the car may at one stage have been earmarked for Tokyo Drift)—this Paul Walker–driven Evolution VII is offered with its Norwegian title, customs documentation, a copy of its 2016 dyno test, and a Carfax report. Also included are text messages from Craig Lieberman confirming: "JMYSNCT9A1U000797 – Verified. Stunt #1."
A highly authentic and exceptionally significant screen-used car from one of the most influential automotive films of the twenty-first century.

Constructed as per Universal Pictures' Back to the Future Part II (1989), this full-scale "Hill Valley Police Cruiser" represents one of the most distinctive vehicles from the film's futuristic 2015 setting. Designed by concept artist Tim Flattery and fabricated by legendary custom builder Gene Winfield, it would be one of only two examples created and the only car built upon a Pontiac Fiero chassis with a fully operational drivetrain, enabling it to move independently for exterior and practical filming.
Sculpted at Winfield's Mojave workshop, the car's fibreglass body features aircraft-inspired contours, integrated light bars, and a distinctive enclosed cockpit canopy. Its advanced aesthetic perfectly captured the film's playful yet visionary depiction of the future.
After the release of the movie, the car remained in Winfield's personal collection before being restored for the Back to the Future 30th anniversary in 2015. It was subsequently displayed at the Petersen Automotive Museum in Los Angeles as part of the acclaimed Hollywood Dream Machines exhibition, alongside some of cinema's most celebrated vehicles.
Purchased directly from Gene Winfield by Movie Cars Central, today, the cruiser remains in largely original configuration, showcasing the unique craftsmanship and design ingenuity that helped shape Back to the Future Part II's enduring legacy. While it would benefit from cosmetic and mechanical work, it remains an instantly recognisable screen-used prop ideal for any serious film or pop-culture collection.
Sold on a bill of sale and accompanied by a Certificate of Authenticity signed by Gene Winfield himself, this is a prop vehicle not intended for road use.

• Accompanied by its UK V5 registration and documentation confirming provenance from Vehicle Effects

Originally produced at the Jefferson plant, this 1970 Dodge Charger left the factory equipped with a 383ci V8 engine. It was later acquired by Universal City Studios for use in Furious 7 (2015), where it was prepared by Dennis McCarthy and his team at Vehicle Effects Inc.—the creative force behind the franchise's most recognisable cars.
Re-engineered for demanding stunt work, the Charger was fitted with a modern 6.2-litre Chevrolet LS3 V8, a functional transmission, reinforced suspension, and a full roll cage. A non-functional blower was added to replicate Dominic Toretto's iconic look while allowing the car to perform reliably during repeated takes. Additional fabrication included production-specific rig mounts and adjustments required for rooftop driving and the vehicle-to-vehicle jump sequence.
Following completion of principal photography, the car was sold directly by Vehicle Effects to Fast & Furious Live, Universal's officially licensed touring stunt show. For stage use, it was fitted with more classic wheels to resemble Toretto's Charger from the first film. Acquired by Movie Cars Central in 2019, the car still retains production markings—including the Fast Live checklist on the passenger-side door—and remains in its film-used configuration.
Offered with its UK V5 and the chain of provenance documents, including the bill of sale from Universal City Studios LLC to Vehicle Effects Inc., and the subsequent bill of sale to Fast Live Productions.
The car will require mechanical recommissioning prior to use: the LS3 engine block shows a crack on one side and a water leak due to freezing damage. While the car runs, repair or replacement of the engine block is advised.
Alongside the Toyota Supra and Nissan Skyline, the Dodge Charger stands among the most emblematic vehicles of the Fast & Furious saga—an instantly recognisable symbol of Dominic Toretto and of the franchise's heritage.

Originally built on 28 January 1969 at Ford's Metuchen plant, this Mustang Mach 1 was specified as a two-door SportsRoof model with the 351ci 4V V8 engine, finished in Black Jade with matching black knit vinyl Mach 1 Hi-Back bucket seats. Factory options included a 3.25 Traction-Lok rear axle, FMX Select Shift automatic transmission, power front disc brakes, and power steering—details verified by the accompanying Marti Report.
Later acquired by Jerry Immersi for the production of John Wick: Chapter 2 (2017), the car was extensively modified for stunt work, including the installation of a roof-mounted driving rig for precision camera coordination and complex chase choreography. When the first stunt Mustang was destroyed during the failed warehouse jump, this car was adapted—its roof rig removed—and used to complete the successful take seen in the final cut of the film. It also appears in subsequent chase scenes, identifiable by its missing driver's door and visible continuity damage.
Mechanically, it remains a genuine M-code Mach 1 with its original 351ci V8 engine, reinforced chassis, and roll-caged interior. Visible traces of filming, including screw holes on the roof, underbody rig mounts, and subtle production reinforcements, all confirm its direct use on set.
This authentic 1969 Ford Mustang Mach 1 is one of the most significant surviving stunt vehicles from John Wick: Chapter 2, directly linked to Keanu Reeves and the franchise's most memorable opening sequence.
Offered with its Marti Report, Certificate of Authenticity from Jerry Immersi, exported US title, and 846A customs document. Although previously driven across the United States by the Movie Cars Central team, the car will require recommissioning before road use: the oil pan (a new replacement is supplied) must be installed, and the front suspension realigned following impact sustained during filming.

REGISTRATION_NO.: None CHASIS_NO.: VF38BXFZE80843171 YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1999 DESCRIPTION:
• Screen-used in Taxi 2 (2000) as a hero/stunt 406 V6
• Built by Christian Bonnichon for the production and driven by rally legend Jean Ragnotti during filming
• Ex-Musée de l'Aventure Peugeot (Sochaux); sold at auction and acquired by Movie Cars Central in 2018
• Signed on the car by Jean Ragnotti (stunt driver) and Samy Naceri (lead actor)
• Powered by a 3.0-litre V6 24-valve engine paired with a five-speed manual gearbox

Originally finished in Gris Quartz with a velour interior, this 1999 Peugeot 406 V6 was produced as a second-series example equipped with the desirable 3.0-litre 24-valve engine and five-speed manual transmission. Ahead of filming for Taxi 2 (2000), the car was delivered to Christian Bonnichon—Peugeot's long-standing film-preparation specialist—to be transformed into one of the film's "hero-stunt" 406s used for high-speed sequences and close-up shots.
The car was extensively reworked to match the now-legendary "transformed" taxi configuration. It received the complete aerodynamic body kit, distinctive TSW Imola alloy wheels, and the signature bright white paint finish. The interior was similarly modified with bespoke leather upholstery and electric front seats. A racing-style "Alain Prost" steering wheel replaced the standard unit, and the gear lever was reimagined in "aircraft" style. The sun visors conceal a control panel, and the rear compartment even features the humorous motion-sickness ("vomit") bags seen on screen. The suspension was lowered, and the floors and sills were adapted to accommodate the deployable plane-style wings featured in the airport chase scene.
For filming, Luc Besson's production team enlisted renowned rally driver Jean Ragnotti, who performed many of the film's key driving sequences. Ragnotti later signed the car's right-hand mirror, while lead actor Samy Naceri also added his signature—making this example uniquely tied to both the film and its stars.
After filming and subsequent promotional use, the car entered Peugeot's official heritage collection, Musée de l'Aventure Peugeot, in Sochaux. It remained there until 2018, when it was sold at the museum's auction and acquired by Movie Cars Central. The car retains its original film bodywork and distinctive presentation as seen on screen.
Showing fewer than 3,400 kilometres from new, this cult 406 remains one of the most authentic surviving examples of France's most famous movie car.
Offered on a bill of sale and accompanied by an insurance valuation, it would require servicing before being driven.

Made famous by the critically acclaimed television series Breaking Bad, the Fleetwood Bounder RV became an enduring pop-culture symbol of Walter White's transformation from chemistry teacher to meth kingpin. This 1986 example has been finished in the same beige-and-brown colour scheme and fitted with a Chevrolet Big Block V8 engine. Although not a production-used unit, it stands as one of the most recognisable vehicles of the TV-series. Acquired by Movie Cars Central from a private collector in France, it remains immediately recognizable as a piece of television history.
Sold on a bill of sale, this Fleetwood Bounder would require recommissioning prior to be driven.

• Accompanied by a Certificate of Authenticity signed by Bob Hartwig
• Acquired directly from Cinema Vehicles, Los Angeles

This 1963 GMC C20 was used on screen during the filming of Ghostbusters: Afterlife (2021). Specially prepared for the production, it was modified to represent the Shandor Mining Co. truck driven by Egon Spengler in the film's dramatic opening sequence, in which he flees through the countryside pursued by a ghost.
Following production, the vehicle was released by Cinema Vehicles, the renowned Los Angeles-based supplier responsible for much of the film's transport and prop vehicles. It was subsequently acquired by Movie Cars Central and brought to France, where it has been displayed since.
Powered by a 305 cubic inch V8 engine coupled to an automatic transmission, the truck remains in its filming configuration, showing only light production wear and a genuine screen-used patina.
Sold on a bill of sale and accompanied by its Certificate of Authenticity signed by Bob Hartwig, President of Movie Machines LLC, this is a genuine piece of cinematic history from one of the most iconic film franchises of all time.

This Cagiva W16 600 Military is a faithful evocation of the dual-purpose motorcycle ridden by Pierce Brosnan as James Bond in the 1995 film GoldenEye. Based on the Italian-built Cagiva platform used by the production, the machine is finished in military olive drab and fitted with equipment appropriate to the on-screen bike, including crash guards, cargo racks, and all-terrain tyres.
Powered by a 598 cc single-cylinder engine mated to a five-speed gearbox, the W16 is both lightweight and robust, capturing the utilitarian aesthetic of Bond's dramatic chase and escape sequence. Acquired by Movie Cars Central from a private collector in Italy, it has been preserved in exhibition condition as a cinematic tribute to one of 007's most memorable action moments.
Showing 15.572km on the odometer, and sold with a copy of its Italian title, this Cagiva will require recommissioning prior to be ridden.

REGISTRATION_NO.: None CHASIS_NO.: N YEAR_MANUFACTURED: 1992 DESCRIPTION:
• Official Warner Bros. Batmobile, constructed circa 1992 for use in the Batman Stunt Show at Six Flags Great Adventure (New Jersey).
• Moulded using the original 1989 Tim Burton "Batman" Batmobile body moulds, preserving the exact dimensions and detailing of Anton Furst's Academy Award–winning design.
• Powered by a Volkswagen Beetle engine, allowing limited drive functionality for live-action performances.
• Built under Warner Bros. license for Six Flags Entertainment as part of the first generation of officially sanctioned Batmobiles produced for promotional and stunt use.
• Retains its fibreglass bodywork, cockpit canopy, and stage lighting features as fitted for show operation.
• Acquired by Movie Cars Central from a private U.S. collector following its retirement from the Six Flags attraction.

Constructed circa 1992 under official Warner Bros. supervision, this Batmobile was created for the Batman Stunt Show at Six Flags Great Adventure. The design reproduces the celebrated 1989 Tim Burton Batmobile, originally designed by Anton Furst for Warner Bros.' feature film. Using the original production moulds, the body was cast in fibreglass and mounted over a practical chassis powered by a Volkswagen Beetle engine, giving the car limited but functional mobility during live performances.
The vehicle was used throughout the Six Flags show's 1992 season, appearing in stunt sequences and stage demonstrations. There, Batman was seen arriving in the Batmobile assisted with Robin, getting out of the car as it is still driving, to go and fight against the Joker. The crow was then seeing the Batmobile leaving by itself with no driver visible. Indeed, the real driver was seating in the back of the car, behind the cockpit and was seeing through a net.
Acquired in a movie related private collection by Movie Cars Central, it remains today in its original show configuration, with its authentic Warner Bros. provenance and distinctive display presence intact. It will be sold with a bill of sale.
